title: Senior's toolkit: measuring and tuning EF Core
summary: Count the queries, split them, pool contexts, page with keys, retry transient failures and watch EF Core's live counters.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: measuring and tuning EF Core
steps.body: EF Core performance work starts with measuring: how many commands did this request run, and how long did each take? These are the tools experienced developers use to find the problem and the switches they change to fix it.

toolkit.what: Log only executed SQL commands, each with its duration. Count the lines for one request to spot an N+1.
flags: one event per command that ran
every event EF Core raises has an id you can filter on

toolkit.what: Make split queries the default for the whole context, then opt single queries back in with `AsSingleQuery()` where one JOIN is better.
Reuse context instances across requests instead of building a new one each time. Helps busy APIs; the context must not keep per-request state in its own fields.
flags: pooling for code that creates contexts itself, such as background jobs

toolkit.what: Keyset (seek) paging: continue after the last key seen. Stays fast on page 5,000, where `Skip(100000)` makes the database read and throw away 100,000 rows.
flags: or a key plus a tie-breaker such as `(Date, Id)`
so the seek is an index range scan

toolkit.what: Retry commands that failed for transient reasons (a failover, a dropped connection) on SQL Server, Azure SQL or PostgreSQL. With it on, wrap your own transactions in the execution strategy.
flags: run a manual transaction so the whole block is retried
toolkit.example: o.UseSqlServer(cs, sql => sql.EnableRetryOnFailure(maxRetryCount: 5, maxRetryDelay: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10), errorNumbersToAdd: null));

toolkit.what: Generate a compiled model so a context with hundreds of entities starts faster. Regenerate it whenever the model changes.
toolkit.example: dotnet ef dbcontext optimize -o CompiledModels -n Shop.Data.CompiledModels
toolkit.when: start-up time is dominated by building the model

toolkit.what: Watch live counters in a running app: queries per second, SaveChanges per second, query cache hit rate, active contexts.
flags: (`--name`) attach to the process by name

steps.prompt: With command logging on, one call to `GET /orders` prints 51 `Executed DbCommand` lines: one for the orders and one per order for its customer. What is the fix?
options: Load the customers in the same query, with `Include(o => o.Customer)` or a `Select` projection that reads `o.Customer.Name`
Make the 50 queries run in parallel
steps.explain: That is the N+1 pattern, usually from lazy loading or a query inside a loop. One query (or two with split queries) replaces 51 round trips. Pooling and retries do not change the number of queries.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the problem it addresses.
pairs: how many commands a request runs
row explosion from several collection Includes
the cost of creating a context per request
deep pages that get slower and slower
slow start-up with a very large model

steps.prompt: Return the next page of orders after the last id the client saw.
steps.explain: Filter past the last key, order by that key, take one page. No `Skip`: the database seeks straight to the right place in the index.

steps.prompt: After turning on `EnableRetryOnFailure`, this code throws `InvalidOperationException: The configured execution strategy 'SqlServerRetryingExecutionStrategy' does not support user-initiated transactions.` What is the fix?
code: await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
options: Run the whole block inside `db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteAsync(...)` so a retry repeats the entire transaction
steps.explain: A retry in the middle of your transaction could repeat half of it. The execution strategy runs your delegate again from the start, so the transaction is retried as one unit.

steps.prompt: Measure first, or change a setting?
buckets: Measure: find out what is happening
Change: the fix once you know
items: Log executed commands for one request

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: For any endpoint that feels slow, count its commands and read its SQL before changing code; most fixes are fewer queries, fewer columns or a missing index. Keep pooling, retries and compiled models for when measurements show the cost is really there.
